Series::CalcAccessor::diff.ito¶

Back to Series::CalcAccessor API Reference

Signatures¶

What It Computes¶

If X is an Itô process, dX = μ dt + σ dW, then a smooth function g(X) is again an Itô process, and Itô’s lemma gives its coefficients:

drift      = g'(x) μ + ½ g''(x) σ²
diffusion  = g'(x) σ

ito computes both without a hand-written formula for g' or g''. It differentiates g by the same automatic-differentiation engine as diff: one reverse pass for the gradient and, for the second-order term, one more pass per state. The extra ½ g'' σ² is the whole difference from the ordinary chain rule; it exists because the squared increment of a Brownian path is its elapsed time, not zero.

The receiver holds the states. Every element is an independent point, so one call evaluates the differential on a whole grid, or for a whole batch of independent processes. g therefore has to act elementwise: the value of g at one element may not depend on another element. mu has the receiver’s shape.

With several states (other, or others), the multivariate formula applies. The second-order term is ½ Σ_ij ∂²g/∂x_i∂x_j · σ_i · σ_j, so the covariation of two states enters through the dot product of their volatility rows. That is why all states in one call must share the same Brownian factors, and why sigma of every state has the same trailing length.

The Result¶

Series::ItoDifferential has these members:

Shape

Meaning

receiver

g at the point

drift

receiver

diffusion

the coefficient of each Brownian factor (m = 1 for a single factor)

g(x + z_k) − g(x) for each jump atom; undefined without jumps

Parameters¶

  • g maps the state (or states) to the function value, elementwise. For the general form it receives the states as a std::vector<Series>, in the order receiver followed by others; with options.time set, its first element is the time.

  • mu is the drift of the receiver, with the receiver’s shape.

  • sigma is the volatility of the receiver. With one Brownian factor it has the receiver’s shape. With m factors it has the receiver’s shape plus a trailing axis of length m. A state driven by one factor and a state driven by two cannot be mixed in one call: give both the same trailing length, using zeros for the factor a state does not load on.

  • other (Series::ItoState{x, mu, sigma}) is the second state. x has the receiver’s shape.

  • jumps (Series::JumpMeasure{sizes, intensity, compensated}) is the jump part, described below.

  • options.time is a Series of times. When set, g’s first argument is the time, and the drift gains the partial time derivative ∂g/∂t.

  • ito_at(time, g, mu, sigma) is the one-state, time-dependent special case.

Jumps¶

A jump of size z does not need a derivative: it moves g(X) by g(x + z) − g(x), however rough g is. A jump part is therefore given as an atomic measure: atom k jumps by sizes[0][k] at rate intensity[k] per unit time. A compound Poisson process with rate λ and jump law p_k has intensity[k] = λ p_k; a Lévy measure with a density is represented by quadrature atoms and weights.

compensated

X contains

Drift of g(X)

false

the sum of the jumps

the continuous part only; the jumps are reported in jump_sizes

true

the jumps minus their mean, a martingale

the continuous part plus Σ ν_k [g(x + z_k) − g(x) − g'(x) z_k]

Examples¶

Example 1. One state, one Brownian factor. For g(x) = x² the lemma gives drift 2xμ + σ² and diffusion 2xσ.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, -0.3});
auto mu = pluss::make_series({0.1, 0.2, -0.1});
auto sigma = pluss::make_series({0.3, 0.5, 0.2});

auto d = x.calc.diff.ito([](const pluss::Series& s) { return s.mul(s); }, mu, sigma);

std::cout << "value     " << d.value << "\n";
std::cout << "drift     " << d.drift << "\n";
std::cout << "diffusion " << d.diffusion << "\n";

Output¶

value     pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.25, 1, 0.09]
drift     pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.19, 0.65, 0.1]
diffusion pluss::Series(shape=[3,1], strides=[1,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.3],
  [1],
  [-0.12]]

Example 2. Several Brownian factors. Give sigma a trailing axis of length m; the second-order term sums the squared loadings and the diffusion gains one column per factor.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0});
auto mu = pluss::make_series({0.1, 0.2});
auto sigma = pluss::make_series({{0.3, 0.1}, {0.5, 0.2}});  // [2 states, 2 factors]

auto d = x.calc.diff.ito([](const pluss::Series& s) { return s.mul(s); }, mu, sigma);

std::cout << "drift     " << d.drift << "\n";
std::cout << "diffusion " << d.diffusion << "\n";

Output¶

drift     pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0.2, 0.69]
diffusion pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.3, 0.1],
  [1, 0.4]]

Example 3. A function of two states. The covariation term depends on how the two volatility rows line up. Here X loads only on the first factor and Y on both, so d[X, Y] = σ_x · σ_y dt.

auto x = pluss::make_series({2.0});
auto mu_x = pluss::make_series({0.05});
auto sigma_x = pluss::make_series({{0.3, 0.0}});

pluss::Series::ItoState y{pluss::make_series({1.5}), pluss::make_series({0.08}),
                          pluss::make_series({{0.24, 0.32}})};

auto g = [](const pluss::Series& a, const pluss::Series& b) { return a.sub(b).pow(2.0); };
auto d = x.calc.diff.ito(g, mu_x, sigma_x, y);

std::cout << "drift     " << d.drift << "\n";
std::cout << "diffusion " << d.diffusion << "\n";

Output¶

drift     pluss::Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[0.076]
diffusion pluss::Series(shape=[1,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.06, -0.32]]

Example 4. ito_product and ito_quotient are the named special cases. The product rule is d(XY) = X dY + Y dX + d[X, Y].

auto x = pluss::make_series({2.0});
auto mu_x = pluss::make_series({0.05});
auto sigma_x = pluss::make_series({{0.3, 0.0}});
pluss::Series::ItoState y{pluss::make_series({1.5}), pluss::make_series({0.08}),
                          pluss::make_series({{0.24, 0.32}})};

auto product = x.calc.diff.ito_product(mu_x, sigma_x, y);
auto quotient = x.calc.diff.ito_quotient(mu_x, sigma_x, y);

std::cout << "product drift  " << product.drift << "\n";
std::cout << "  X mu_y + Y mu_x + cov = " << 2.0 * 0.08 + 1.5 * 0.05 + 0.3 * 0.24 << "\n";
std::cout << "quotient drift " << quotient.drift << "\n";

Output¶

product drift  pluss::Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[0.307]
  X mu_y + Y mu_x + cov = 0.307
quotient drift pluss::Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[0.025037037]

Example 5. Time-dependent functions go through ito_at. Discounting g(t, x) = e^(−rt) x has drift e^(−rt)(μ − r x), which vanishes exactly for a process growing at the rate r.

const double r = 0.03;
auto x = pluss::make_series({100.0, 80.0});
auto mu = pluss::make_series({r * 100.0, 0.07 * 80.0});
auto sigma = x.mul(0.2);
auto time = pluss::make_series(0.8);

auto d = x.calc.diff.ito_at(
    time, [r](const pluss::Series& t, const pluss::Series& s) { return s.mul(t.mul(-r).exp()); }, mu, sigma);

std::cout << "discounted drift " << d.drift << "\n";

Output¶

discounted drift pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 3.1241143]

Example 6. Any number of states, with the time passed through the options. The function receives the states in a vector, preceded by the time.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0});
auto mu = pluss::make_series({0.1});
auto sigma = pluss::make_series({{0.2, 0.0}});
std::vector<pluss::Series::ItoState> others = {
    {pluss::make_series({2.0}), pluss::make_series({0.05}), pluss::make_series({{0.0, 0.3}})},
    {pluss::make_series({3.0}), pluss::make_series({0.02}), pluss::make_series({{0.1, 0.1}})}};

pluss::Series::ItoOptions options;
options.time = pluss::make_series(0.5);

// g(t, x, y, z) = t x y z
auto d = x.calc.diff.ito(
    [](const std::vector<pluss::Series>& v) { return v[0].mul(v[1]).mul(v[2]).mul(v[3]); }, mu, sigma, others,
    nullptr, options);

std::cout << "drift     " << d.drift << "\n";
std::cout << "diffusion " << d.diffusion << "\n";

Output¶

drift     pluss::Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[6.43]
diffusion pluss::Series(shape=[1,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.7, 0.55]]

Example 7. Raw and compensated jumps. Two atoms, jumps of +0.4 at rate 2 and −0.7 at rate 1. The raw form leaves the drift alone and reports the effect of each jump; the compensated form adds the integral of g(x + z) − g(x) − g'(x) z.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.5});
auto mu = pluss::make_series({0.1});
auto sigma = pluss::make_series({0.3});
auto square = [](const pluss::Series& s) { return s.mul(s); };

pluss::Series::JumpMeasure jumps;
jumps.sizes = {pluss::make_series({0.4, -0.7})};
jumps.intensity = pluss::make_series({2.0, 1.0});

jumps.compensated = false;
auto raw = x.calc.diff.ito(square, mu, sigma, jumps);
jumps.compensated = true;
auto compensated = x.calc.diff.ito(square, mu, sigma, jumps);

std::cout << "raw drift         " << raw.drift << "\n";
std::cout << "jump sizes        " << raw.jump_sizes << "\n";
std::cout << "compensated drift " << compensated.drift << "\n";
std::cout << "check: 0.19 + 2*0.16 + 1*0.49 = " << 2 * 1.5 * 0.1 + 0.09 + 2 * 0.16 + 0.49 << "\n";

Output¶

raw drift         pluss::Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[0.39]
jump sizes        pluss::Series(shape=[2,1], strides=[1,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[[1.36],
  [-1.61]]
compensated drift pluss::Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[1.2]
check: 0.19 + 2*0.16 + 1*0.49 = 1.2

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • g must be elementwise. A function that mixes elements of the receiver (a sum, a cumulative sum, a matrix product) is not an independent copy of one state per element. The second-order term is read off the diagonal of the Hessian, so cross-element dependence is silently dropped rather than detected. Reduce after the call, not inside g.

  • The same factors for every state. The covariation term is the dot product of volatility rows, which only means something when the rows refer to the same Brownian motions. A mismatched trailing length is rejected.

  • The result is a differential, not a path. ito returns the coefficients of dt and dW at a point. Simulating the process, or integrating the differential along a path, is a separate step (see antidiff.ito).

  • Raw and compensated jump parts are different processes. Choosing the wrong one shifts the drift by the mean jump contribution.

Example 8. Misuse is rejected with a message naming the problem. A volatility whose shape does not match the receiver, in this case:

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0});
auto mu = pluss::make_series({0.1, 0.2});
auto sigma = pluss::make_series({0.3, 0.4, 0.5});

try {
  auto d = x.calc.diff.ito([](const pluss::Series& s) { return s.mul(s); }, mu, sigma);
  std::cout << d.drift << "\n";
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string message = e.what();
  std::cout << "error: " << message.substr(0, message.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

error: Series.calc.diff.ito: sigma must have the shape of the state, or the shape of the state followed by one axis of Brownian factors

Summary¶

diff.ito is Itô’s lemma for any smooth function of one or several Itô processes, with Brownian and jump parts, computed by automatic differentiation. Give it g and the coefficients; it returns the coefficients of g(X).

  • diff.marcus: the differential when jumps follow a flow.

  • antidiff.ito: stochastic integrals along a path.
